Vignette: Priya

Priya is a fifty-year-old South Asian woman who has spent the better part of her adult life navigating the careful, measured world of diplomacy. She carries herself with the kind of composure that comes from decades of representing her country in rooms where every word matters. She is precise, controlled, and professionally accomplished - qualities that have served her well and that she now leans on, perhaps too heavily, to hold herself together.

Three years ago, Priya was stationed at a consulate in a mid-sized European city when a cleaning contractor inadvertently introduced an industrial chemical solvent into the building's ventilation system. Within minutes of arriving at her desk that morning, she noticed a sharp, acrid smell she couldn't identify. Before she could act on the instinct that something was wrong, she was overcome - eyes burning, throat closing, her body dropping to the floor of her office before she could reach the door. She regained consciousness in a hospital, where she was told she had sustained a significant chemical inhalation injury. Two junior colleagues were hospitalized alongside her. One of them did not fully recover.

In the months that followed, Priya returned to work. She told herself she was fine. There were cables to draft, meetings to attend, a career she had built with extraordinary discipline. But something had shifted in ways she found difficult to name and more difficult to admit.

She now notices that she cannot enter a room without first scanning for the nearest exit. When she walks into any enclosed space - a conference room, a restaurant, even her own apartment - there is a beat of something close to panic before she locates the door. She has rearranged her home office so that her desk faces the window, which she keeps cracked open regardless of the weather. Colleagues have commented on it. She laughs it off.

Certain smells stop her completely. Cleaning products, industrial solvents, even the sharp scent of a colleague's hand sanitizer can pull her back to that morning with a vividness that feels less like memory and more like reliving. Her throat tightens. Her vision narrows. She has learned to excuse herself quickly and stand outside until the sensation passes, which she describes as "clearing her head." She does not call it what it is.

Sleep is fragmented and unreliable. She wakes in the early hours with her heart hammering, the details of the dream already dissolving but the physical dread fully intact. She lies still and waits for it to pass, which it does, eventually. She has started keeping the television on through the night as background noise - something she finds embarrassing and cannot entirely explain.

What troubles Priya most is not the intrusions themselves but what they have done to the version of herself she has always known. She was someone who moved through the world with confidence and purpose. Now she feels, beneath the polished surface she presents, a persistent low-grade vigilance that exhausts her. She is irritable in ways she monitors carefully. She has declined two postings in the past eighteen months, citing scheduling conflicts. The truth, which she has not said aloud until recently, is that she was afraid of being far from home, far from hospitals, far from the exits she has memorized.

She describes the experience of that morning not with dramatic language but with a quiet, almost clinical detachment that occasionally cracks. She says she felt, for the first time in her adult life, completely powerless - not over a negotiation or a political outcome, but over her own body, in her own office, on an ordinary Tuesday. That, she says, is what she cannot seem to get past. The ordinariness of it. The fact that she never saw it coming.
